title: Irrigation Coverage Calculator: Sprinkler Area
description: Work out the area one sprinkler or pivot covers with the Irrigation Coverage Calculator — from throw radius to square feet and acres. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a sprinkler with a 40 ft throw covers approx. 5,027 sq ft — about 0.115 acres — before overlap with its neighbours is designed in.
quick_answer: The Irrigation Coverage Calculator turns a sprinkler's throw radius into the area it waters: πr² in square feet, square metres and acres. Enter the radius your head actually achieves and read its coverage — the figure spacing decisions, zone counts and water budgets are all built from.
steps_intro: One head, one circle. Systems are just circles arranged honestly:

body.t: Heads are spaced for head-to-head coverage — each sprinkler's throw reaching the next. This area per head is the unit the layout multiplies.
A lawn's area divided by a head's honest coverage (with overlap allowed for) estimates the head count — then pressure and flow, via the
A pivot is this calculator at farm scale: its radius is the machine's length, its coverage the field's watered circle — corners handled separately, as always.
Coverage × depth is volume. Knowing each zone's area is the only way a water bill forecast means anything.
Throw 40 ft: coverage = π × 40² ≈ 5,026.5 sq ft (0.115 ac). A 10,000 sq ft lawn needs at least two heads' worth of circle — three or four in practice, once corners and overlap have their say.
Throw 15 m: coverage ≈ 706.9 m². Metric systems design in the same circles; only the units on the nozzle box change.

faq: The circular area a sprinkler covers from its throw radius: πr², reported in sq ft, m² and acres.
Can I use the result for professional work?
For layout planning and estimates, yes. Final designs also model pressure variation, wind drift and overlap patterns — this is the geometric layer of that work.
Why do heads need to overlap?
A sprinkler's application falls off toward its edge, so single-coverage areas are under-watered at the rim. Head-to-head spacing (spacing ≈ radius) overlaps the weak edges into uniformity.
What radius do I enter — rated or achieved?
Achieved, at your working pressure. Rated throw is measured in still air at full pressure; your system's real number is the honest input.
Multiply the full-circle result by the arc fraction (a 180° head covers half). The calculator gives the full circle; the fraction is your setting.
How does this relate to flow volume?
Coverage area × application depth = volume per session. The Irrigation Flow Volume Calculator approaches the same session from the flow-rate side.
My pressure is low — what happens?
Throw shrinks, so coverage shrinks with the square of the loss: 10% less radius is about 19% less area. Enter the achieved radius, not the catalogue one.
Triangular (offset) spacing covers ground more evenly at the same radius. The per-head area here is the input either way; the layout pattern decides uniformity.
